titre: Left and Right (1789): A Matter of Seats in the Hall, According to Gauville
accroche: In August 1789, a deputy of the nobility notes how the supporters of the king grouped themselves to the right of the president.
contenu_vulgarise:
“Left” and “right” are used today to classify parties in almost every country. The labels come from a testimony of a few lines left by a deputy of the nobility, the baron de Gauville, in the journal he kept during the Constituent Assembly, which would be published only in 1864.

## A Scene in a Hall, Not a Doctrine

Gauville writes: “On the 29th, we were beginning to recognize one another: those who were attached to their religion and to the king had stationed themselves to the right of the president, in order to avoid the shouts, the remarks, and the indecencies that were going on in the opposite part.” The reason he gives is practical: getting away from the noise. He names no program and no camp; he speaks of seats in the hall, located in relation to the president's chair. Historians date this scene to the end of August 1789, when the Assembly was debating the king's place in the future constitution.

## Who Sits Where

His count is precise: “about a hundred and fifty members of the clergy, as many of the nobility, and eighty of the Third Estate,” that is, about 380 deputies on the right. The group therefore does not coincide with a single order: elected members of the Third Estate sit there too. What unites them, according to him, is attachment to religion and to the king. The day before, Gauville says, he had insisted, with others, that the Catholic religion be declared the state religion, without success and amid jeers. A few days later, the speakers turn “more particularly to the question of the royal sanction,” that is, to the king's power over laws.

He also tells his own case. He had tried to change seats in order to remain master of his opinion, but “I was obliged to abandon the left side absolutely, or else I was condemned to always vote there alone and consequently condemned to the jeers of the galleries.” Sitting somewhere already amounted to announcing one's vote.

## The Shift

The label is thus born of a group reflex, not of a classification of ideas: elected members group together to be among themselves, and those across from them become, in Gauville's own pen, “the left side.” These words have outlived the hall, regimes, and borders, even though their content has changed several times. In 1789, they separate the supporters of maintaining royal power from those who want to limit it. That is not the division the words designate today, and timeless definitions of the right and the left make us forget this origin.

One question remains that Gauville's journal leaves open: from what point did a mere arrangement of seats become a way of saying who one is?

repere.texte: Gauville counts, to the right of the president, “about a hundred and fifty members of the clergy, as many of the nobility, and eighty of the Third Estate,” that is, about 380 deputies (a sum added by the editors from his count).
repere.source: Journal du baron de Gauville (Journal of the baron de Gauville) (published 1864), Internet Archive scan

carte.punch: “Right” and “left”: at the start, seats in a hall.
carte.idee: At the end of August 1789, the baron de Gauville notes that the supporters of religion and the king have placed themselves to the right of the president, to flee the noise. The label comes from an arrangement of seats, not from a program.

quiz.question: According to Gauville's journal, why do deputies place themselves to the right of the president?
choix: The Assembly's rules reserved the right for the nobility and the left for the Third Estate
To stay among supporters of religion and the king, away from the shouts on the opposite side
The presiding officer had assigned them that part of the hall by lot
Supporters of the republic had settled there first, out of concern for order
quiz.explication: Gauville gives a practical reason: to group together among those attached to religion and the king, to avoid the shouts from the other side. No rule imposed it, and the group also included 80 elected members of the Third Estate.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When was the baron de Gauville's journal published?
choix: In 1792, after the fall of the king
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The journal was kept during the Constituent Assembly but appeared only in 1864: it is a rediscovered testimony, not a text circulated at the time.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does Gauville say he abandoned the left side of the hall?
choix: The president had expelled him from it after a quarrel
He had been elected by the Third Estate and had to sit with it
He would always have voted alone there, amid the jeers of the galleries
He wanted to move closer to the chair to hear better
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Gauville explains that he was obliged to leave the left, otherwise condemned to always vote there alone and endure the jeers of the galleries.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the entry, who separates the right side from the left side in 1789?
choix: Catholics and Protestants in the Assembly
Supporters of maintaining royal power and those who want to limit it
Supporters of free trade and those of protectionism
Deputies from Paris and those from the provinces
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 1789, the words separate the supporters of maintaining royal power from those who want to limit it, far from the meaning left and right have today.
